scenarios.title: The prerequisite audit
scenarios.situation: A sophomore asks you how to prepare for quant internships. Their coursework so far: one semester of calculus, an intro stats class that never covered joint distributions, and a Python course focused on web scraping. They want to start grinding interview brainteasers immediately.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right first move?
choices: Audit and close the math gaps first — multivariable calculus, linear algebra, and probability through conditional expectation — before interview prep, because every quant interview question sits on top of that foundation.
Start with brainteasers; interview performance matters more than coursework depth.
Switch to a finance major immediately; the degree name is what recruiters screen for.
Learn C++ first; speed of implementation is the binding constraint.
scenarios.why: Quant interviews test probability, statistics, linear algebra, and calculus under time pressure. A student who cannot compute a conditional expectation or diagonalize a matrix will fail the interview regardless of how many puzzles they've memorized. The audit maps exactly which prerequisites are missing so study time goes to the binding constraint — the math, not the puzzles.
scenarios.hint: What do the brainteasers assume you already know?

scenarios.title: The internship map
scenarios.situation: A junior with strong math grades asks when to apply for quant trading and research internships. They assume the timeline matches regular software engineering recruiting — applications in the fall of junior year, interviews in winter — and plan to start preparing next summer.
scenarios.prompt: What should you tell them about the quant recruiting timeline?
choices: Quant recruiting runs much earlier than general SWE: applications and interviews for top firms typically happen in the summer and early fall, a full year before the internship — so preparation must start now, not next summer.
The timeline is identical to SWE; their plan is fine.
Internships don't matter for quant; only graduate school admissions do.
They should wait until senior year when they have more coursework.
scenarios.why: Quant funds and trading firms run accelerated, early pipelines — many interview in late summer/early fall for the following summer's internship. A junior who waits until the standard SWE timeline finds the quant seats already filled. The map matters because the preparation (probability depth, mental math, programming) must be done before the window opens, not during it.
scenarios.hint: If interviews happen a year before the internship, when must preparation be finished?

scenarios.title: Conditional expectation under pressure
scenarios.situation: In a mock interview you're asked: a fair coin is flipped until the first head appears. You are paid $2^n where n is the number of flips. Then a twist: you may stop the game at any time before the flip and take a fixed $3 instead. The interviewer wants the fair value of the game with the stop option.
scenarios.prompt: How do you reason about it?
choices: Compute the conditional expectation of continuing at each state: after k tails the expected remaining value doubles each flip while the stop value is fixed, so the optimal policy and the game's value come from comparing E[continue | k tails] against $3 at each decision point — the stop option is worth taking exactly when the conditional expectation of continuing falls below it.
The game is worth infinite dollars because the payoff is unbounded, so the stop option is irrelevant.
The value is $3 because you would always stop immediately.
Flip until the expected payoff exceeds $3, which happens on the first flip.
scenarios.why: This is an optimal-stopping problem in miniature: at each state you compare the conditional expectation of continuing against the certain $3. The naive 'infinite expectation' answer (the St. Petersburg paradox) ignores the decision structure; the interview tests whether you condition on the information you actually have at each decision point. Working the recursion — value at state k = max(3, expected value of flipping once more) — is the whole skill.
scenarios.hint: After one tail, what is the expected value of flipping exactly once more versus stopping?

scenarios.title: The vectorized backtest
scenarios.situation: A candidate shows you a backtest of a mean-reversion strategy written as a Python for-loop over 10 years of minute bars. It takes 40 minutes to run, so they tested 3 parameter sets. They ask whether to optimize the loop with C++.
scenarios.prompt: What is the more important fix?
choices: Vectorize the strategy with array operations (NumPy/pandas) so a run takes seconds, enabling hundreds of parameter trials — but first fix the methodology: the loop likely contains look-ahead bias (using information not available at trade time), which no amount of speed can rescue.
Rewrite in C++; speed is the binding constraint in quant research.
Test more parameter sets on the 40-minute loop; compute is cheap if you run it overnight.
The strategy is mean-reversion so the loop is fine; only high-frequency strategies need vectorization.
scenarios.why: Two problems, in order of importance: correctness, then speed. A 40-minute loop that peeks at future data produces a beautiful, worthless equity curve — look-ahead bias is the classic backtest killer. Once the logic is point-in-time correct, vectorization turns 40 minutes into seconds, which is what actually enables research velocity: the number of ideas you can test per day.
scenarios.hint: How would you check whether the loop uses future information?

scenarios.title: The proctored exam decision
scenarios.situation: You've completed the five graduate courses in an online MicroMasters-style finance credential: modern finance foundations, financial accounting, mathematical methods for quantitative finance, and derivatives markets. The final step is a single proctored comprehensive exam, and you're debating whether the exam is worth the stress and fee.
scenarios.prompt: How should you value the proctored exam?
choices: The verified credential — courses plus the proctored comprehensive exam — is what converts coursework into a signal employers and degree programs recognize; without the exam you have knowledge but no credential, and the degree-pathway value (advanced standing toward a master's) typically requires the full verified MicroMasters.
Skip the exam; the knowledge is what matters and employers never check credentials.
The exam only matters if you want to become a professor.
Retake the easiest course instead; a higher average grade signals more.
scenarios.why: Graduate-level online credentials derive their signaling value from verification: proctored exams prove the work is yours. The MicroMasters model explicitly ties the credential — and any credit or advanced-standing pathway into a master's program — to completing the verified track including the comprehensive exam. Skipping it keeps the learning but forfeits the signal and the pathway option.
scenarios.hint: What does the exam prove that the coursework alone doesn't?

scenarios.title: The career fork
scenarios.situation: A PhD student in applied math has three offers: desk quant at a bank (pricing and hedging exotics, close to trading), quantitative researcher at a fund (alpha research, longer horizons), and a strategy consulting role at a top firm (generalist problem-solving, client-facing). They love stochastic calculus and also love explaining ideas to non-technical audiences.
scenarios.prompt: How should they think about the fork?
choices: Map the roles to what they actually optimize: desk quant = deep derivatives math under trading-floor time pressure; researcher = open-ended statistical modeling with publication-like rigor and slower feedback; consultant = breadth, communication, and business judgment with less technical depth. The right choice follows which daily work — not which prestige — fits their strengths, and the consulting door stays open later than the quant doors.
Take the highest-paying offer; the work converges within two years anyway.
Take consulting; quants burn out and the math is the same everywhere.
Take the desk quant role; researchers never touch real markets.
scenarios.why: The three paths diverge in daily reality: desk quants live inside stochastic calculus and trader requests with intraday deadlines; researchers run longer experiments on noisy data where most ideas fail; consultants trade depth for breadth and client influence. Loving both the math and the explaining is real information — it points toward roles where technical depth meets communication (desk quant facing traders, or consulting with a quant edge) — and the fork is not permanent, but switching costs rise with seniority, so choose on work-content fit first.
scenarios.hint: What does a typical Tuesday look like in each role?
objectives: desk quant vs researcher vs consultant

lessons.title: Quantitative Finance: The Ladder — Core concepts
concepts: The ladder has three rungs: (1) undergraduate preparation — multivariable calculus, linear algebra, probability and statistics at depth, programming; (2) a graduate finance credential — graduate-level finance, accounting, mathematical methods, derivatives — verified by proctored examination; (3) research-level mathematics and interview craft — stochastic calculus, case interviews, and the career fork.

The prerequisite audit is the highest-ROI study activity: list every mathematical topic quant interviews assume (conditional expectation, Bayes, distributions, linear algebra, calculus), rate yourself honestly on each, and attack the weakest first. Interview puzzles are applications of this foundation, not a separate subject.

Probability at depth means conditional reasoning: E[X | information] is the object you actually compute in interviews, trading, and research. Optimal stopping, Bayes' rule, and the law of total expectation are the three moves that solve most interview problems.

Programming for quant means vectorized numerical computing (NumPy/pandas), point-in-time-correct backtests with no look-ahead bias, and enough software engineering to make research reproducible. Speed of iteration beats speed of execution at the research stage.

A MicroMasters-style credential bundles graduate courses with a proctored comprehensive exam; its two values are the employer signal (verified graduate-level work) and the degree pathway (advanced standing toward a master's). Both values require completing the verified track.

The career fork: desk quant (derivatives pricing, hedging, trader-facing, intraday pressure), quantitative researcher (alpha research, statistical rigor, slow feedback, high idea mortality), consultant (breadth, communication, business judgment). Choose on daily-work fit; switching costs compound with seniority.

example.code:
import numpy as np

def gbm_paths(S0, mu, sigma, T, steps, n_paths, seed=0):
    # Vectorized geometric Brownian motion: the quant research workhorse
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    dt = T / steps
    Z = rng.standard_normal((n_paths, steps))
    # Exact discretization: log returns are normal with mean (mu - .5 s^2) dt
    log_rets = (mu - 0.5 * sigma ** 2) * dt + sigma * np.sqrt(dt) * Z
    S = S0 * np.exp(np.cumsum(log_rets, axis=1))
    return np.column_stack([np.full(n_paths, S0), S])

paths = gbm_paths(100, 0.05, 0.2, 1.0, 252, 100_000)
print(f"E[S_T] ~ {paths[:, -1].mean():.2f}  (theory: {100*np.exp(0.05):.2f})")
example.walkthrough: One vectorized call simulates 100,000 paths — this is the research-velocity pattern from the backtest scenario: array operations replace the 40-minute loop. The exact log-normal discretization avoids discretization bias, and comparing the simulated E[S_T] against the closed form 100·e^0.05 validates the simulation before you trust it for pricing.

pitfalls: Common trap: grinding puzzles before the audit. Every interview question is applied probability and linear algebra — without the foundation, puzzle practice has no surface to stick to.
Common trap: treating the credential as the goal. The MicroMasters-style pathway is a signal and a degree option; the underlying graduate finance knowledge is what interviews actually test.
Common trap: backtesting with look-ahead bias. If your simulation uses any information not available at the decision time, the result is fiction — point-in-time correctness comes before speed.
Common trap: choosing the fork on prestige. Desk quant, researcher, and consultant optimize different daily realities; pick the work content you'll still enjoy on a bad Tuesday.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Prerequisite audit worksheet
labs.objective: Build and run a self-scoring prerequisite audit: a Python script listing the core quant-interview math topics, where you rate each 0–3 and the script reports your weakest areas and a study priority order.
steps: Create audit.py with a list of at least 12 topics: conditional expectation, Bayes' rule, common distributions, law of total expectation, eigenvalues, matrix diagonalization, multivariable calculus, Taylor series, hypothesis testing, regression, random walks, and the central limit theorem.
Add a ratings dict where you score yourself 0 (never seen) to 3 (could teach it) on each topic — be honest; this is for you.
Make the script print topics sorted weakest-first with a suggested weekly hour allocation proportional to the gap.
Run the script and save its output to audit_results.txt.
Pick your bottom 3 topics and write the first concrete study action for each in study_plan.txt.

checks.hint: Print a labeled priority ordering so the audit output is readable.
Write study_plan.txt with your bottom-3 topics and first actions.

labs.title: Vectorized Monte Carlo pricer
labs.objective: Implement the vectorized GBM pricer from the lesson, price a European call by Monte Carlo, and validate against the closed-form Black-Scholes price to prove the simulation is trustworthy.
steps: Create mc_pricer.py with the vectorized gbm_paths function from the lesson example.
Price a 1-year European call (S=100, K=100, r=5%, sigma=20%) by averaging discounted payoffs over 200,000 paths; print the Monte Carlo price.
Implement the closed-form Black-Scholes call price (standard normal CDF via math.erf) and print it beside the Monte Carlo estimate.
Confirm the two agree within simulation noise (a few cents), then halve the paths and note how the error grows — record both in RESULTS.txt.
Add a one-paragraph note in RESULTS.txt: why validating against a closed form is mandatory before using Monte Carlo on exotics with no closed form.

checks.hint: Label the Monte Carlo price line clearly.
Print the closed-form price labeled 'Black-Scholes' for comparison.

sections.title: Quantitative Finance: The Ladder — Core path

behavioral.prompt: Why quantitative finance? Why not software engineering or data science?
points: Name the specific moment or problem that pulled you toward quant (a probability course, a pricing puzzle, a market microstructure rabbit hole)
Connect it to what the work actually is: decisions under uncertainty, expressed mathematically, tested against markets
Distinguish from adjacent fields: quants live at the intersection of stochastic modeling and P&L in a way SWE and DS roles don't
pitfalls: 'For the money' as the lead answer
Generic praise of math with no finance connection
No distinction from data science

behavioral.prompt: Walk me through your preparation plan for quant interviews.
points: Describe the prerequisite audit: how you mapped the required math and found your gaps
Name the resources and the weekly structure (problems per day, mock interviews, programming reps)
Give evidence it's working: a topic you couldn't do a month ago that you can do now
pitfalls: 'Just grinding puzzles' with no structure
No honest gap assessment
No measurable progress to point to

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to learn a large body of technical material on a deadline.
points: Set the deadline and the stakes: what depended on learning it in time
Show the system: how you broke the material down, sequenced it, and verified understanding
Quantify the outcome and name the study method you'd reuse
pitfalls: A story with no real deadline pressure
Cramming presented as a system
No verification step described

behavioral.prompt: Explain a difficult technical concept — say, risk-neutral pricing — to a non-technical stakeholder.
points: Lead with the intuition (replication: the price is what the hedging portfolio costs)
Use one concrete number example, not symbols
Check understanding by inviting the stakeholder's restatement
pitfalls: Drowning them in notation
Condescension disguised as simplification
No check for understanding

behavioral.prompt: Describe a research or coding project where your first approach failed.
points: Describe the failed approach and the evidence that killed it (not just a feeling)
Explain the pivot: what the failure taught you about the problem
Show the second approach succeeding — or explain why you stopped, if stopping was right
pitfalls: A failure with no real cost
Blaming tools or teammates
No lesson extracted

behavioral.prompt: How do you handle the pressure of a timed case interview or trading-floor deadline?
points: Name your concrete technique: structured decomposition, writing down assumptions, time-boxing
Give an example where it worked under real pressure
Acknowledge what still stresses you and how you manage it
pitfalls: 'I thrive under pressure' with no evidence
No actual technique named
Claiming pressure never affects you

behavioral.prompt: Where do you see the desk quant vs. researcher vs. consultant fork taking you, and why?
points: Show you understand what each role's daily work actually is
Connect your demonstrated strengths to one path's demands
Name what you'd need to develop for the others — and keep the door honest, not flattering
pitfalls: Choosing on prestige or pay alone
Claiming you'd be equally great at all three
No understanding of the daily work differences

behavioral.prompt: What is the biggest gap in your quant preparation right now, and what are you doing about it?
points: Name the gap precisely (a topic, not 'more experience')
Show the plan already in motion: resources, schedule, milestones
Give the date you'll close it and how you'll verify
pitfalls: A humblebrag disguised as a gap
No plan — just awareness
A gap so large it undermines the whole candidacy

simulations.title: Why Did the Backtest Lie?
simulations.brief: Your momentum strategy shows a 2.1 Sharpe in backtest and loses money live. Diagnose the gap.

steps.symptom: Backtest Sharpe 2.1 (2018–2023). Live trading: -4% in two months. Same code.
evidence: Survivorship-biased equity universe (only stocks still listed in 2023)
Backtest assumed zero slippage, zero fees
Average slippage 8 bps per trade; strategy trades 400x/year
options: The market regime changed — wait for mean reversion
Look-ahead and cost bias: survivorship bias inflated returns, and 400 trades/year × 8 bps slippage eats the entire edge — the backtest never modeled reality
Increase leverage to recover the losses
steps.explain: Two classic lies: survivorship bias (dead stocks don't drag the backtest) and frictionless trading (400 × 8bps ≈ 3.2%/year of phantom edge). Honest backtests use point-in-time universes and real cost models.

steps.symptom: You rebuild with a point-in-time universe and 10 bps all-in costs. Sharpe drops to 0.9. Is the strategy dead?
options: Viable at small scale: 0.9 Sharpe with contained drawdowns is a real edge if sized honestly and kept under capacity
Add leverage until the Sharpe looks good again
steps.explain: 0.9 honest Sharpe is a tradeable edge at appropriate size. The ladder lesson: most 'dead' strategies were never alive (biased), and most 'mediocre' honest ones are careers. Size to capacity, not to dreams.

steps.symptom: What's the permanent research practice this incident demands?
evidence: Must prevent biased backtests from reaching production again
Every future strategy gets the honest treatment by default
options: Only trade strategies with backtest Sharpe above 2.0
A research checklist enforced in code: point-in-time data, survivorship-free universe, cost model, out-of-sample holdout, and a pre-registered hypothesis
Hire a consultant to bless each backtest
steps.explain: Process beats brilliance: pre-register the hypothesis (no p-hacking), enforce point-in-time data and costs in the pipeline, and keep a true holdout. The checklist is the junior quant's senior.

simulations.debrief: Backtests lie by bias (survivorship, look-ahead) and by omission (costs). The professional standard: honest data, honest costs, pre-registered hypotheses, and sizing to measured capacity.

simulations.title: Two Offers
simulations.brief: You're a junior quant with two offers: a bank's prestigious rotational program, or a 12-person prop shop. Choose the ladder.

steps.text: Offer A: bulge-bracket bank, rotational program, famous name, $180k, slow promotion, heavy process. Offer B: 12-person prop shop, $150k + real P&L cut, you ship to production in month two, unknown name. Your career goal: become a genuinely good quant.

choices.label: Take the bank — prestige compounds and the name opens doors forever
choices.feedback: Prestige is real currency, but two years of rotational PowerPoint teaches you process, not P&L. You'll know the bank's politics intimately and trading barely at all.

choices.label: Take the prop shop — P&L responsibility early is the fastest teacher
choices.feedback: Month two, your code has real money on it. Every mistake costs basis points you feel personally. Nothing teaches like P&L.

choices.label: Negotiate the bank up and take whichever pays more
choices.feedback: Optimizing year-one comp is the classic junior mistake — the learning rate, not the salary, determines year-five comp.

steps.text: Eighteen months at the bank: you've rotated through three desks, built exactly one model that traded (briefly), and your bonus was formulaic. A prop shop calls. What now?

choices.label: Stay — you're up for Associate and the pension vests
choices.feedback: The golden handcuffs close one link at a time. In five years you'll be a well-paid process expert who has never owned risk.

choices.label: Leave now — the 18 months bought you just enough credibility to get the prop seat, and the learning clock is ticking
choices.feedback: Correct late is better than comfortable forever. You banked the brand name; now go buy the skill.

steps.text: Year one at the prop shop: your first strategy made money, your second lost $200k in a week (a bug, not the market). The partners are watching. How do you handle the post-mortem?

choices.label: Blame the market regime — the strategy was sound
choices.feedback: It was a bug, and everyone knows it. Denial at a prop shop is a career-ending move — trust is the only currency.

choices.label: Own the bug completely, present the fixed validation pipeline, and show the checklist that would have caught it
choices.feedback: Prop shops forgive bugs; they don't forgive cover-ups. The post-mortem with a systemic fix is how juniors become seniors.

simulations.debrief: The ladder isn't prestige — it's P&L proximity. Choose the seat closest to real risk earliest, own mistakes completely, and let the learning rate (not year-one comp) drive the decision.

simulations.title: Climb the Ladder
simulations.brief: Order the quant career climb from undergraduate preparation to senior quant readiness.

steps.context: The full climb, honestly mapped. Put the stages in order.
items: Undergraduate foundation: probability, statistics, linear algebra, programming
Graduate credential: financial mathematics / statistics / CS with real projects
Junior seat: own a small piece of production risk, learn the cost of mistakes
Mid-level: own a strategy or book end-to-end — research, risk, and P&L
Senior: allocate capital and mentor — your edge is now other people's growth

simulations.debrief: Math, credential, production scar tissue, ownership, then leverage through others. The fork is real (bank vs. prop vs. tech), but the ladder's rungs don't change.

simulations.title: Audit the Resume
simulations.brief: A junior quant's resume is one hiring-manager skim away from the bin. Find the 3 lines that kill it.

steps.config:
# resume.conf — junior quant
sharpe_claim = 3.2 (backtest)     # line 2
pnl_attribution = 'team P&L'        # line 3
skills = python, pandas, excel       # line 4
projects = coursework only          # line 5
references = 'available on request' # line 6
github = empty                       # line 7
contact = professional              # line 8

issues.description: Sharpe 3.2 claimed from a backtest with no mention of costs, universe, or out-of-sample — every hiring manager reads this as bias, not edge.
issues.fix: sharpe_claim = '1.1 (point-in-time universe, 10bps costs, 2yr out-of-sample)' — honest numbers beat big ones.

issues.description: 'Team P&L' with no personal attribution — the reader assumes your contribution was zero.
issues.fix: pnl_attribution = 'owned signal X: +$180k net of costs, 2024' — name your slice.

issues.description: Coursework-only projects — every applicant has coursework; none of it traded.
issues.fix: projects = 'independent backtest engine on GitHub with honest cost model' — show, don't list.

simulations.debrief: Lines 4, 6, 7, 8 are neutral or fixable. The killers: an unqualified backtest Sharpe, unattributed P&L, and zero evidence of independent work. Quant hiring managers read resumes as research papers — methods section required.

simulations.title: The Interview Loop
simulations.brief: Final round at a top fund. The interviewer slides a brainteaser across the table — then watches HOW you think.

steps.text: 'You have a biased coin with unknown bias. How do you simulate a fair coin?' You know the von Neumann answer. What's the winning response structure?

choices.label: Blurt the answer immediately — speed impresses
choices.feedback: Speed without structure looks memorized. They wanted to see reasoning, and you showed recall.

choices.label: Think aloud: define the goal, propose flip-pairs, derive why HT/TH are equiprobable, note the efficiency cost
choices.feedback: The full performance: problem framing, derivation, AND the practical caveat (expected flips). That's a quant thinking, not reciting.

choices.label: 'I'd look it up — in practice I'd just use a library.'
choices.feedback: Honest, but the interview tests reasoning under uncertainty — the actual job. Libraries don't save you when the library is wrong.

steps.text: Follow-up: 'Now the bias drifts over time. Your von Neumann trick breaks. What now?' You're off-balance. Recover how?

choices.label: Guess: 'Use more flips?'
choices.feedback: Guessing under pressure is the opposite of the job. The interviewer notes it.

choices.label: Rebuild from first principles aloud: 'The trick needs stationarity — with drift I'd estimate the bias in windows and...'
choices.feedback: Recovery by method: you named the broken assumption and rebuilt. Interviewers remember recoveries more than perfect runs.

steps.text: The interviewer leans in: 'Good. Now — when would you NOT use the fair coin even if you could build it?'

choices.label: 'When the cost of flips exceeds the value of fairness — e.g., low-stakes decisions where bias doesn't matter.'
choices.feedback: You reached for the meta-question: engineering is cost-benefit, not purity. The interviewer smiles — that's the senior answer.

choices.label: 'Never — fairness is always worth it.'
choices.feedback: Absolutism in a quant interview is a red flag. Everything has a price, including elegance.

simulations.debrief: Quant interviews test reasoning structure, not recall: think aloud, name your assumptions, derive, then price the solution. And when you stumble, rebuild from first principles — recovery is the real test.

consoleSims.debrief: On a trading desk, the queue IS risk management: log the deviation, assign an owner, move it now. Slippage doesn't wait for the next sprint.

consoleSims.title: Ship the Research Pipeline
consoleSims.brief: Research code ships through the same gates as everything else. Trigger, fix, configure, approve.

tasks.instruction: Trigger a new build of the research pipeline.
Retry the failed 'test' stage (the backtest validation suite).
Set variable COST_MODEL_BPS to 10 — the honest cost model is now pipeline-enforced.

consoleSims.debrief: The research checklist from sim-1 lives here as pipeline: enforced cost models, validation suites, human approval before production. Process is the senior you don't have yet.

terminalMissions.title: Survey the Desk
terminalMissions.brief: Orient on the research workstation: list files, read the notes.
terminalMissions.success_message: Desk surveyed. Know your data before you trade on it.

terminalMissions.title: Record the Fills
terminalMissions.brief: Log today's fills to fills.txt — the research journal starts here.

checks.hint: Type: echo "AAPL +120bps" > fills.txt (no output on success).

terminalMissions.success_message: Fills recorded. The journal is the difference between trading and gambling.

terminalMissions.title: Attribute the P&L
terminalMissions.brief: Count your fills and isolate the winners — attribution in the shell.
terminalMissions.success_message: Attributed. Every basis point named, every fill owned.

terminalMissions.title: Seal the Hypothesis
terminalMissions.brief: Pre-register your hypothesis with a hash — no p-hacking after the fact.

checks.hint: Type: sha256sum momentum 12-1 formation — the real hash plus your hypothesis are echoed.

terminalMissions.success_message: Hypothesis sealed. Pre-registration is what separates research from storytelling.

terminalMissions.title: Check Colocation Latency
terminalMissions.brief: Verify the network path to the exchange: DNS and round-trip.
terminalMissions.success_message: Path verified. In this business, milliseconds are money — verify the road.

terminalMissions.title: Audit the Research Logs
terminalMissions.brief: The strategy's runtime log holds the truth. Read its edges and hunt errors.
terminalMissions.success_message: Logs audited. The live system grades your backtest daily — read the grades.

terminalMissions.title: Verify the Environment
terminalMissions.brief: Confirm the research environment: identity and home directory.
terminalMissions.success_message: Environment verified. Reproducibility starts with knowing where you stand.

videos.title: The Backtest That Lied
videos.blurb: In-sample: +38% a year. Go-live: -4%. The backtest was overfit to history — walk-forward validation or walk away from the strategy. (Preview — narration coming; voiceover pending TTS restore.)

videos.title: Returns Are Vanity, Sharpe Is Sanity
videos.blurb: Strategy A returns 8% with 20% volatility; B returns 6% with 8% — Sharpe 0.40 vs 0.75. B earns less and keeps more of it. (Preview — narration coming; voiceover pending TTS restore.)

videos.title: The Drawdown
videos.blurb: March: up 22%, the PM is mentally buying a boat. June: down 30% from the peak, investors redeem at the bottom — size for the worst day. (Preview — narration coming; voiceover pending TTS restore.)
